title: To whom shall we go (John 6:60–69)
hook: many walk away; Peter says thou hast the words of eternal life

segments.voice: Yesterday, the words the crowd argued over: my flesh is meat indeed. Your line was eat, and live. And a new week begins.

It ends in a synagogue in Capernaum, where John says Jesus taught all of it: the bread, the flesh, the blood. And it costs him. Not the hillside crowd this time: his own disciples, people who had been following him, start to leave. Some of them may have eaten the loaves by the lake. Jesus watches them go. He doesn't run after them with a softer version. Then he turns to the twelve still standing there and asks a question that leaves the door wide open.
screen: `A SYNAGOGUE IN CAPERNAUM.` → `HIS OWN DISCIPLES WALK OUT.` → `HE TURNS TO THE TWELVE.`

segments.voice: It starts with a complaint, in the Douay-Rheims: "This saying is hard, and who can hear it?" Not just hard to understand. Hard to accept. Jesus knows they're murmuring, and he doesn't take it back. His words, he says, are spirit and life, and some of them don't believe. Then: "After this many of his disciples went back; and walked no more with him." Jesus turns to the twelve: "Will you also go away?" Not a threat. A real question. He lets them choose. And Peter answers, first and from the gut: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." Notice what Peter doesn't say. Not, I understand it all now. Not, it isn't hard. Not even, I'm sure. Just: where else would we go? It's the faith of someone who has looked at the alternatives and can't walk away from these words. Then he adds: we have believed and have known that thou art the Christ, the Son of God. Some Catholics turn to this line on days when the teaching is hard, or the Church is hard to love, or God is silent. Staying isn't the same as having no questions. Peter will deny Jesus three times before the story ends. But here, when it costs something, he stays.
screen: `THIS SAYING IS HARD.` · `MANY WALKED NO MORE WITH HIM.` · `WILL YOU ALSO GO AWAY?` · `WHERE ELSE WOULD WE GO?` · then, large: `THOU HAST THE WORDS OF ETERNAL LIFE.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're tempted to walk away from, a commitment, a friendship, a hard conversation, maybe even this path, and don't decide anything; just stay with it for now, noticing the urge to get up and go without following it. If you pray, use Peter's words, Lord, to whom shall we go; if not, notice what staying feels like.
Peter. The one who answered first and from the gut when Jesus asked the twelve if they too would leave: Lord, to whom shall we go? Today's word.
Your line: words of eternal life. Staying, with the questions still open. Day five hundred five, in the books.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Peter's answer on the Twenty-first Sunday in Ordinary Time in Year B, the last of the Sundays that read through John 6.

chat.says: Lots of disciples walked away from Jesus in John 6. Why did Peter stay?
options: Not because it was easy: where else would he go? Jesus had the words of eternal life.
Because he finally understood everything Jesus said, so none of it felt hard.
Because Jesus ran after the ones leaving and promised them a softer teaching.
chat.meaning: Peter doesn't claim to understand it all. He says: Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life.

Verse numbering: the Douay runs one higher than the KJV/NABRE in John 6 after 6:51; refs give both. Confirm.

Peter's confession: the Douay (following the Vulgate) reads 'thou art the Christ, the Son of God' in 6:70; many modern critical texts read 'the Holy One of God'. The voice paraphrases the Douay. Consider a note in a later edition.
